name: Iran
system_note: A theocratic republic led by an unelected supreme leader.
snapshot: Ali Khamenei was killed in the opening hours of the US-Israeli assault in February; his son took over, and Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz shook the world economy.
culture: Iran is heir to Persian empires stretching back 2,500 years, and Persian poetry, from Hafez and Rumi to Ferdowsi's Shahnameh, is quoted in daily speech. Nowruz, the spring new year, predates Islam and is the biggest celebration. Iranian cinema, from Abbas Kiarostami to Asghar Farhadi, is internationally acclaimed despite censorship. Persian carpets, gardens and tea houses are cultural staples.
society: Iran has a young, highly educated population, with more women than men in universities, yet faces mandatory hijab laws that sparked the 2022 "Woman, Life, Freedom" protests. Sanctions and mismanagement have driven high inflation and a collapsing currency. The Revolutionary Guard controls large parts of the economy. Ethnic Kurds, Baluch, Azeris and Arabs have their own grievances.
situation: For 37 years, Iran had one supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, who survived wars, sanctions and repeated waves of protest, most recently a nationwide uprising in January 2026. On 28 February, in the opening hours of a joint US-Israeli assault, he was killed along with several senior commanders, reportedly at a meeting about how to crush those protests (Iran International). The Assembly of Experts named his son, Mojtaba, as successor, turning the Islamic Republic's highest office into something close to a hereditary one.

Iran hit back at Israel and at US bases and Gulf states across the region, and above all it closed the Strait of Hormuz, through which about a fifth of the world's oil had passed. Oil prices soared, and countries from Singapore to Belgium felt it. After roughly 40 days, a ceasefire in April led to the highest-level US-Iran talks in half a century, in Islamabad. A preliminary deal followed in June, but it lapsed; strikes and Iranian missile fire resumed over the summer. By late August, Iran's deputy foreign minister was still saying flatly that "the Strait of Hormuz is closed," with ships allowed through only in coordination with Iran, and Tehran and Oman were working on a joint shipping lane and even sharing toll revenue (Al Jazeera via UDLAP). Mojtaba Khamenei, reportedly injured in the first strikes, has not appeared in public since February, communicating through written messages that vow revenge. At home, the regime has tightened its grip, including a harder line on compulsory hijab. Trump said in August he was "not in a hurry" to resume talks.
power: A theocratic republic. The supreme leader, chosen for life by the clerical Assembly of Experts, controls the armed forces, the Revolutionary Guards, the judiciary and state media. An elected president and parliament run day-to-day government, but candidates are vetted by the clerical Guardian Council.
holders: Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, since March 2026; President Masoud Pezeshkian.

update.html: The war is in a tense stalemate. The US blockade of Iranian ports continues, a new US task force targets Iran's land and Caspian routes, and Iran keeps Hormuz all but closed, saying it is mining unauthorised routes. After limited US strikes on Qeshm Island in early November, Trump said on 9 November, after meeting Qatar's prime minister, that Iran was 'militarily effectively over', that there was 'positive momentum' toward a deal and that new strikes were 'quite unlikely'. Tehran says talks depend on seven conditions, including lifting the blockade and sanctions, releasing frozen funds and ending the war on all fronts, and that Hormuz could reopen within two days if they are met. France blamed the Revolutionary Guards on 9 November for cyber sabotage of supermarket fridges and is seeking EU sanctions.
